reasons: The checks and the runner exist, but I did not run them, so I cannot confirm that every entry currently passes.
The file's own description gives counts (45 entries, 69 deterministic checks) that I did not verify.

terms.meaning: Deliberately breaking code in a small way to check whether the tests notice.
One broken version of the code produced by one mutation.
A change that alters the text but not the behaviour, so no test can fail because of it.
The exact piece of text a mutation searches for in its file.
The address pytest uses to name one test, such as a file, a class and a test name.
The Python tool that finds and runs the tests.
The test tool used for the frontend code.
A simple Python record whose fields cannot be changed after it is created.
Stored sample data that tests reuse.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: File purpose and setup
sections.what: Explains why the registry exists and how it is used, then loads the standard tools it needs to define the entries.
sections.why: The top description records the reason for the list: passing tests do not prove the tests would catch a broken mechanism.
sections.watch_out: Each new mechanism needs its own entry here, or it will not be checked.

sections.name: Mutation (part 1)
sections.title: Shape of one mutation entry
sections.what: Defines the record that describes one mutation: its name, file, find text, replacement text, tests that must fail, reason, and an optional equivalence note.
sections.why: Each entry needs the same fields so the runner and the checks can read every entry the same way.
sections.watch_out: The find text must occur exactly once in the file, and the replacement must not already be present, or the runner cannot tell a committed mutation from a moved anchor.

sections.name: Mutation (part 2)
sections.title: Confidence and duplication checks
sections.what: Lists the first group of guarded mechanisms: the penalty for unsupported assumptions, the duplication total check, the evidenced share check, and the check that evidence counts stay within the pack.
sections.why: Each entry's reason field explains what its guard protects.
sections.watch_out: Find text is matched exactly, including spacing, so reformatting these lines breaks their entries.

sections.name: Mutation (part 3)
sections.title: Evidence count and viewer guards
sections.what: Finishes the evidence count entry, then covers three viewer guards: the shared widening floor, the band table columns, and the notice that bands are not comparable across versions.
sections.why: Each entry's reason field records what a reader would be misled into believing without the guard.
sections.watch_out: These entries target frontend files, so a formatting change in the viewer code can break the exact text match.

sections.name: Mutation (part 4)
sections.title: Feature account and agreement rules
sections.what: Lists guards on the feature account: rejecting unknown features, applying the canonical order, and refusing a measured agreement on too few items. It also starts the agreement fallback entry.
sections.why: Each entry's reason field explains how the rule would fail silently if removed.
sections.watch_out: The thinness rule currently has one enforcing producer, so its entry matters more once another producer exists.

sections.name: Mutation (part 5)
sections.title: Agreement fallback and revision carry-over
sections.what: Finishes the agreement fallback entry, then lists a reproduction check that ignores unmeasured features, a confidence count entry, and a check that assumptions carry across revision passes.
sections.why: Each entry's reason field explains what a reviewer would be unable to see if the guard were removed.
sections.watch_out: Find text includes indentation, so changes to nesting in these functions break the entries.

sections.name: Mutation (part 6)
sections.title: Objections and budgets
sections.what: Lists guards that require structural objections to be answered, that the calibration starts from the recorded score, that feasibility breaches are not treated as assumptions, and that revision budgets follow the tier. It starts the strike scoping entry.
sections.why: Each entry's reason field explains the outcome the rule prevents, such as cheap resolutions or wrong budgets.
sections.watch_out: Budget entries depend on the tier table in the pipeline, so changing that table changes what these entries prove.

sections.name: Mutation (part 7)
sections.title: Strike, gap and determinism scoping
sections.what: Finishes the strike entry, then covers guards on per-block gap counts, prerequisite sources, the work unit join key, replay order, and the injected clock.
sections.why: Each entry's reason field explains how a silent change would alter a block, a join, or the repeatability of a run.
sections.watch_out: Replay order and the clock are what make runs repeatable, so changes to them can show up as subtle differences rather than errors.

sections.name: Mutation (part 8)
sections.title: Fingerprints, critic merging and accumulation
sections.what: Covers guards on the checkpoint schema version, the schema fingerprint, critic challenge merging, struck evidence accumulation, and the start of the answered objections entry.
sections.why: Each entry's reason field explains how the rule keeps state correct across passes and across code changes.
sections.watch_out: The fingerprint entry hard-codes an expected value, so changing the schema requires updating that value in the entry.

sections.name: Mutation (part 9)
sections.title: Revision result and prerequisite rules
sections.what: Finishes the answered objections entry, which includes an equivalence note tied to the two-pass budget. Then it covers guards on discarded revision results, prerequisites that cite nothing, and the gate's reading of uncited prerequisites.
sections.why: The equivalence note explains why one mutation can never be caught while the budget stays at two passes.
sections.watch_out: The answered objections entry becomes killable if any tier is ever allowed a third pass, and its note must then be removed.

sections.name: Mutation (part 10)
sections.title: Capacity, input and effort rules
sections.what: Finishes the uncited prerequisite gate entry, then covers the capacity check claim, input validation for golden cases, effort derived from the pack, and the establishment merge by maximum.
sections.why: Each entry's reason field explains a wrong conclusion that the guard prevents.
sections.watch_out: The capacity entry guards against reporting a check as having run when it did not.

sections.name: Mutation (part 11)
sections.title: Input validation and manifest rules
sections.what: Covers the pipeline's validation of cases, reading the optional establishment field, the thawing of the manifest mapping, and a check that every optional field is listed. It starts the enablers double count entry.
sections.why: Each entry's reason field explains a rule the code states but could silently stop honouring.
sections.watch_out: The optional field entry is the calibration for a sweep test, so if it survives, the sweep has stopped being able to fail.

sections.name: Mutation (part 12)
sections.title: Enablers, adoption and run cost
sections.what: Covers the double count of shared enablers, the adoption ramp, the zeroed run cost, and the start of the diagnostic suppression entry.
sections.why: Each entry's reason field explains what a reader of the value figures would be misled about.
sections.watch_out: The run cost entry guards a figure that is often left out of business cases, so it is easy to remove by accident.

sections.name: Mutation (part 13)
sections.title: Rendering, prerequisites and credit caps
sections.what: Finishes the diagnostic suppression entry, then covers the unpriced prerequisites, the credit cap for each process, and the unpriced run cost notice.
sections.why: Each entry's reason field explains how the total or its warning would mislead a reader.
sections.watch_out: The credit cap entry is the one that changes the portfolio total, not just how it is split.

sections.name: Mutation (part 14)
sections.title: Pool validation, phasing and weighting
sections.what: Covers the pool check, the widening that marks unevidenced bands, the phasing of external prerequisites, the value weighting of the evidenced share, and the start of the provenance entry.
sections.why: Each entry's reason field explains a figure that would look right while being wrong.
sections.watch_out: The pool entry compares a field with itself in its replacement, so it only ever passes when the rule is removed.

sections.name: Mutation (part 15)
sections.title: Provenance, budget and fixture protection
sections.what: Finishes the provenance entry, then covers the budget check that counts only the output side, and the guard that stops a live run writing into the recorded fixtures.
sections.why: Each entry's reason field explains how a run becomes impossible to explain later or silently moves its baseline.
sections.watch_out: The fixture entry protects the baseline that all other entries depend on, so a live run that writes there would weaken every other check.

sections.name: Mutation (part 16)
sections.title: Clean tree and commit lock
sections.what: Covers three guards for the runner: refusing to start on a dirty tree, taking the lock that warns about commits, and the value purity gate that stops the value engine importing an LLM library.
sections.why: Each entry's reason field explains how the runner could overwrite work or record a mutation as the source.
sections.watch_out: The lock entry matters only while the runner is patching files, so a change to when the lock is taken can open a window for a bad commit.

summary: Holds the curated list of deliberate breaks. Each entry is one small text swap that disables a safety mechanism, paired with the tests that must fail when the swap is applied.
purpose: Shows whether the tests would notice if an important mechanism stopped working. A passing test suite only shows that the tests agree with the code.
why: Two real defects passed the suite and were caught only by a human reviewer. Listing each important mechanism here with a test that must fail gives a way to catch that gap automatically.
how: Each entry names a file, the exact text to find, the replacement text, the tests that must fail, and a plain reason. The runner in evals/run.py applies each swap in turn, runs the named tests, and reports any entry whose tests stay green. The file itself only defines the list.
inputs: Nothing at runtime. The file is a fixed list of entries that point at source files and test names in the repository.
outputs: A tuple named MUTATIONS made of Mutation records. The runner in evals/run.py and the checks in tests/mutations/test_registry.py read it.
risks: Each entry matches exact text. If a refactor moves, renames or reformats a mechanism, its entry breaks. If a mutation is left in the source by accident, the registry may grade the broken code as correct.
debug: If an entry is reported as broken, check that its find text still appears exactly once in the named file. If the run reports a committed mutation, restore the named file from version control. Run the checks in test_registry.py first, because they test each entry without changing any file.
